questions.prompt: Per Lesson 1, which statement correctly defines data quality according to DAMA's Data Management Body of Knowledge (DMBOK)?
options: The degree to which data is fit for its intended purpose(s)
Data that contains zero errors or typos
Data that is complete, with no NULL values in any column
Data that has been formatted consistently across every system
Data that matches the data type defined in the database schema
Data that has been reviewed and approved by a data governance council
questions.explain: DMBOK defines data quality as the degree to which data is fit for its intended purpose(s) — a judgment relative to a specific use, not an absolute standard. The same dataset can be high quality for one team's use and low quality for another's, using the exact same rows.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the definition the lesson specifically calls out as 'the definition everyone gets wrong.' 'Error-free' sounds reasonable but isn't the actual standard — a dataset can be perfectly formatted and error-free while still being completely unfit for the one thing the business actually needs it for, like an address with a wrong ZIP code that looks flawless but can't reach the customer.

questions.prompt: Match each of Lesson 2's six data quality dimensions to its one-line test.
right: Is anything missing that should be present?
Does the value conform to its defined format/rules?
Does the same fact agree with itself everywhere it's stored?
Does the value match the real-world fact?
Is the data current enough for this decision right now?
Does each real-world entity appear exactly once?
questions.explain: Accuracy asks whether a value matches the real-world fact. Completeness asks whether anything expected is missing. Consistency asks whether the same fact agrees with itself across copies. Validity asks whether a value conforms to a defined rule. Uniqueness asks whether each entity appears exactly once. Timeliness asks whether data is current enough to be useful right now.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Gartner research, as cited in Lesson 3, puts the average cost of poor data quality to organizations at $________ million per year.
questions.explain: Lesson 3 cites Gartner's figure of $12.9 million per year as the average cost of poor data quality to organizations, alongside IBM's separately sourced $3.1 trillion estimate for the cost to the entire U.S. economy.

questions.prompt: Match each of Lesson 4's data quality roles to what it actually does.
right: Anyone who uses the data to do their job, often the first to notice a problem
Business-side leader accountable for a specific data domain
Technical role that implements and runs the checks a steward designs
Hands-on role that translates the owner's intent into concrete rules and definitions
questions.explain: The data owner is the business-side leader accountable for a domain's quality standard. The data steward translates that intent into concrete rules, definitions, and monitoring. The data custodian is the technical role — often a DBA — that implements and runs those checks. The data consumer is anyone acting on the data, often the first informal signal that something's wrong.

questions.prompt: Put Lesson 5's five stages of the data quality lifecycle in the correct order.
items: Profile — discover what's actually in the data, with no judgment yet
Define — turn profiling findings into explicit rules and thresholds
Measure — run the rules against real data, repeatedly, and track results over time
Remediate — fix bad records and trace back to the root cause
Monitor — keep watching continuously so the next problem is caught early
questions.explain: The lifecycle runs profile, then define, then measure, then remediate, then monitor — and then loops back to profile again as new data and systems arrive. Skipping straight to 'define' without profiling first is the most common mistake, since rules written on assumption rather than what the data actually contains tend to fail against real data.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about data profiling, per Lesson 6.
options: Profiling describes what data actually contains without judging whether that's good or bad
Deciding that a 3% NULL rate is unacceptable is part of the 'profile' stage, not the 'define' stage
Column profiling looks at one column at a time: NULL rate, distinct values, min/max
Relationship profiling checks whether foreign keys across tables actually match up
A table showing up in Object Explorer confirms the data inside it is good quality
questions.explain: Profiling is discovery, not judgment — it reports facts like 'this column is 3% NULL' without deciding whether that's acceptable, which is the define stage's job. Column profiling works one column at a time; relationship profiling checks whether foreign keys actually match across tables. A table appearing in Object Explorer only confirms it exists, telling you nothing about whether its contents are any good.

questions.code:
SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS total_rows,
    SUM(CASE WHEN EmailAddress IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS null_emails,
    100 * SUM(CASE WHEN EmailAddress IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS null_email_pct
FROM Sales.Customer;
questions.prompt: A developer wrote this query to calculate a NULL percentage but used 100 instead of 100.0. If null_emails is 42 out of 8,400 total_rows (a true rate of exactly 0.5%), what does null_email_pct actually return, and why?
options: 0 — 100 * 42 / 8400 is evaluated as integer division in T-SQL, which truncates the true 0.5 result down to 0
0.5 — T-SQL always returns decimal precision regardless of the literal's type
An error — dividing by COUNT(*) is not allowed in a SELECT list
50 — because 100 * 42 equals 4200, and 4200 / 8400 is read directly as a percent
questions.explain: Lesson 7 warns that T-SQL performs integer division when every operand is an integer, silently truncating the decimal portion. 100 * 42 = 4200, and 4200 / 8400 in integer division truncates to 0, not 0.5. Multiplying by 100.0 instead of 100 forces decimal division and produces the correct 0.50 result.

questions.code:
SELECT
    OrderStatus,
    COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
GROUP BY OrderStatus
ORDER BY row_count DESC;
questions.prompt: This frequency-distribution query returns Shipped (8,210), Pending (640), Cancelled (190), and Shipp3d (3). What does the presence of 'Shipp3d' most likely indicate, and which dimension does it point to?
options: A validity problem — a typo'd value that slipped past the expected set of allowed OrderStatus values
A completeness problem — three rows are missing their OrderStatus entirely
A timeliness problem — those three rows haven't been refreshed recently
Not a real issue — GROUP BY always returns at least one unexpected row on large tables
questions.explain: Lesson 8 uses this exact scenario: a frequency distribution surfacing 'Shipp3d' alongside the expected Shipped, Pending, and Cancelled values is a validity problem — a value that doesn't belong to the column's allowed domain, caught directly by a profiling query before it's ever formalized as a Chapter 4 rule.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 9, a child-table row whose foreign key value has no matching row in the parent table is called an ________ row.
questions.explain: An orphaned row is a child-table row pointing to a parent key that doesn't exist. The standard way to profile this with T-SQL is a LEFT JOIN from child to parent, filtered to rows where the parent side came back NULL.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement from Lesson 10's four questions to ask of every profiling finding.
options: A 2% NULL rate might be completely normal on an optional field but a real problem on a required one
The raw violation count matters more than what percentage of the table it represents
A NULL rate that jumped from 0.5% to 3% last week is a different conversation than one steady at 3% for a year
A finding is only actionable if some specific person can specifically act on it
Profiling results should always be reported as raw counts, never percentages, to avoid misleading stakeholders
questions.explain: Lesson 10's four questions are: is this actually abnormal, what's the scale, is this new or longstanding, and who needs to know and what decision does it change. The scale question specifically warns that the same raw count can mean 'edge case' or 'fundamentally broken' depending entirely on the denominator — so the percentage, not just the raw count, is what matters, and reporting only raw counts would miss that.

questions.prompt: A customer record lists the phone number 555-0199, which is validly formatted. A support agent later discovers this is not actually the customer's current number. What does this reveal about the relationship between accuracy and validity, per Lesson 11?
options: The number can be fully valid (correct format) while still being inaccurate (not the real-world fact) — validity and accuracy are different dimensions
The number cannot be valid if it is inaccurate, since validity already accounts for real-world truth
This is purely a completeness problem, since the field has a value present
Accuracy and validity are the same test performed at two different stages of the same check
questions.explain: Validity is checked against rules — format, type, range, domain. Accuracy is checked against truth — does the value reflect the real-world fact. A value can be perfectly valid and still be wrong, exactly as 555-0199 is a validly formatted US phone number whether or not it's actually this customer's number.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the three disguises of 'missing' data covered in Lesson 12.
options: NULL is the easiest kind of missing value to detect, since IS NULL catches it directly
An empty string ('') is automatically caught by an IS NULL check
A sentinel value like 'N/A' or '1900-01-01' looks like real data to a naive COUNT, but functionally means the same thing as missing
A completeness check that only looks for NULL will accurately capture all the ways data can be missing
Record-level completeness asks whether an entire expected record exists at all, not just a single field
questions.explain: NULL is the database's own 'no value' marker and the easiest to detect. An empty string is not NULL, so IS NULL misses it entirely — it needs its own check. A sentinel value like 'N/A' or a default date disguises missing data as real data to a naive COUNT. A completeness check that only checks IS NULL therefore systematically undercounts missingness. Record-level completeness is the separate question of whether an entire expected record exists at all, distinct from field-level completeness.

questions.prompt: Match each Lesson 13 scenario to whether it's internal consistency (within one table/row) or cross-system consistency (between two systems).
left: OrderDate is before the customer's own SignupDate, checked within one Orders/Customers join
A customer's Email in the CRM differs from their Email in the billing system
State and ZipCode disagree within the same Customers row
Loyalty tier stored as 'Gold' in the e-commerce system and as '1' in the POS system
questions.explain: Internal consistency checks agreement between related columns within one row or table — OrderDate vs. SignupDate, or State vs. ZipCode. Cross-system consistency checks the same fact as stored in two genuinely separate systems — CRM email vs. billing email, or a loyalty tier represented differently in e-commerce vs. POS.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 14, a validity rule requiring OrderStatus to be one of 'Pending', 'Shipped', 'Cancelled', or 'Returned' is an example of a ________ rule — one requiring the value to be a member of a fixed, allowed set.
questions.explain: A domain (allowed-value) rule requires a value to be one of a fixed set of legal values. Lesson 14 names four kinds of validity rule: type, format, range, and domain — a domain violation looks like Status = 'Pending-ish' when only a specific fixed set of values is legal.

questions.prompt: Email 'j.lee@example.com' appears on three rows: CustomerId 101, 205, and 310. Which rows does this query return for that email, per Lesson 15's de-duplication pattern?
options: CustomerId 205 and 310 — every row for that email except the first by CustomerId order
CustomerId 101 only — the first occurrence
All three rows (101, 205, 310)
No rows — ROW_NUMBER() only applies to numeric columns, not text
questions.explain: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Email ORDER BY CustomerId) numbers each email group starting at 1, ordered by CustomerId. CustomerId 101 gets rn = 1, 205 gets rn = 2, and 310 gets rn = 3. Filtering to rn > 1 keeps every row in the group except the first — exactly the pattern used as the starting point for a de-duplication delete.

questions.prompt: An inventory count was captured correctly and refreshed 2 hours ago, well within a 24-hour freshness threshold. But the system that captures it takes 6 hours to reflect a sale after it happens. Which timeliness problem does this describe, per Lesson 16?
options: A latency problem — the gap between a real-world sale happening and that event reaching the system is too long, even though the data was recently refreshed
A freshness problem — the data is already more than 24 hours old
An accuracy problem — the inventory count itself is factually wrong
Not a timeliness issue at all, since the refresh happened only 2 hours ago
questions.explain: Lesson 16 distinguishes freshness (how old the data is, relative to its expected update cadence) from latency (how long it took a real-world event to reach the data). This scenario passes the freshness check but fails on latency — the pipeline's 6-hour delay between the sale happening and it appearing in the system is a timeliness failure measured by latency, not freshness.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 17, what are the four parts that turn a one-off SQL query into a documented, repeatable data quality rule?
options: Scope, condition, severity, and owner
Table name, column name, data type, and primary key
Author, date written, line count, and database name
Severity, priority, deadline, and budget
Scope, condition, index, and execution time
Owner, approver, reviewer, and auditor
questions.explain: A well-documented rule has four parts: scope (what table/columns it applies to), condition (what makes a row pass or fail), severity (how bad a failure is), and owner (who gets notified and decides what 'fixed' means). Skipping any of these turns the rule back into a one-off query — a condition without a severity makes every failure look equally urgent, and a rule without an owner means failures pile up with nobody responsible.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E keeps two of the four correct parts — scope and condition — but swaps severity and owner for index and execution time, which are performance-tuning concerns, not the documentation structure Lesson 17 defines. A rule can be well-documented without ever mentioning an index, but it isn't a rule at all without a severity and an owner.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Lesson 18's best practices for writing SQL data quality checks.
options: A data quality check should only query data, never update or delete it
WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2024 is just as SARGable as WHERE OrderDate >= '2024-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2025-01-01'
When UNION ALL-ing keys of different data types across rules, casting them consistently avoids an error or a slow implicit conversion
The WHERE clause in a check query should describe the condition that makes a row BAD, not the condition that makes it good
Heavy checks should always run during business hours so failures are caught immediately
questions.explain: Checks should stay read-only, leaving remediation as a separate, deliberate step. Casting UNION ALL keys consistently avoids type-mismatch errors or slow implicit conversions. The lesson specifically recommends writing the WHERE clause for the failure condition, not the success condition. Wrapping an indexed column in a function like YEAR() makes a WHERE clause non-SARGable, unlike an equivalent range comparison — the two are not equally index-friendly. Heavy checks should be scheduled outside business hours, not during peak traffic.

questions.code:
SELECT o.OrderId, o.CustomerId
FROM dbo.Orders AS o
LEFT JOIN dbo.Customers AS c
    ON o.CustomerId = c.CustomerId
WHERE c.CustomerId IS NULL;
questions.prompt: This referential integrity check is missing the 'AND o.CustomerId IS NOT NULL' condition from Lesson 19's recommended pattern. For a guest-checkout order where CustomerId is intentionally NULL, what happens?
options: That guest order is incorrectly flagged as an orphaned row, even though a NULL foreign key there means 'no customer, intentionally,' not a broken reference
Nothing changes — NULL foreign keys are automatically excluded by the LEFT JOIN itself
The query raises an error, because c.CustomerId IS NULL can't be evaluated against a NULL input
The guest order is excluded from the results entirely, the same as if the condition were present
questions.explain: Lesson 19 specifically warns that AND o.CustomerId IS NOT NULL matters: without it, a legitimately NULL foreign key (a guest checkout, intentionally with no customer) gets caught by the same c.CustomerId IS NULL filter as a genuine orphan, because the LEFT JOIN also returns no match for a NULL join key. That's a completeness question, not an orphan, and the query without the extra condition can't tell the two apart.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about reconciliation checks, per Lesson 20.
options: Row counts can match perfectly between two systems while a sum reconciliation still fails, because the right number of rows can carry the wrong values
Count reconciliation and sum reconciliation always catch the exact same failures
A reconciliation mismatch tells you the two systems disagree, but not which one is correct or why
A linked server lets a query reference another server's database directly, without needing a staged local copy
Reconciliation checks are only useful at the individual-row level, never at the aggregate level
questions.explain: Sums catch a different failure mode than counts — the right number of rows with corrupted or mis-mapped values, such as a currency conversion applied twice. A reconciliation mismatch is a symptom, not a diagnosis: it tells you the systems disagree, not which side is right or why. A linked server queries another server's database directly as an alternative to staging a local copy. Reconciliation is specifically an aggregate-level check (counts, sums), scaled up from row-level consistency checking, not limited to individual rows.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 21, a ________ band is an expected range around a value — such as 950 to 1,050 for a daily order count — where values outside it in either direction trigger a failure, unlike a hard threshold's single line.
questions.explain: A tolerance band suits checks where both too high and too low are suspicious, such as a sudden volume spike meaning a duplicate load, not just a drop meaning a missed one — unlike a hard threshold, which is a single line that fails once crossed in one direction.

questions.prompt: A SQL Server Agent job step runs this check, with the RAISERROR call from Lesson 22's pattern removed and replaced by a plain SELECT, as shown. When the threshold is actually exceeded, what happens in SQL Server Agent's job history?
options: The job step shows as Succeeded, because a SELECT that returns rows doesn't itself raise an error, even though the data genuinely violates the threshold
The job step shows as Failed, because Agent treats any returned rows as a failure signal automatically
The job refuses to run at all, because HAVING without GROUP BY is invalid syntax
SQL Server Agent emails the operator automatically whenever a SELECT returns at least one row
questions.explain: Lesson 22 is explicit that a job step only shows as Failed when the T-SQL it ran raises an error, such as with RAISERROR or THROW, or returns a non-zero exit code. A plain SELECT that returns violating rows doesn't do either — the step reports Succeeded even though the threshold was crossed, which is exactly why the lesson insists on RAISERROR to make the failure loud enough for a notification to fire.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about root cause analysis, per Lesson 23.
options: A root cause is the upstream reason a symptom exists, not the bad value itself
Remediation without root cause analysis means cleaning the same category of bad data over and over
Root causes fall into one of four categories: people, process, technology, or source data
The 5 Whys technique is finished as soon as the first 'why' produces any answer at all
Grouping a rule's failures by a likely driver, like source system or entry channel, can point directly at a root cause
questions.explain: A symptom is what a rule detects — a null, a duplicate, an out-of-range value. A root cause is the upstream reason it exists, sorting into people, process, technology, or source data. Remediation without finding the cause is a treadmill: the same category of bad data keeps recurring. 5 Whys means repeatedly asking why, usually around five times, not stopping at the first answer — the first 'why' almost never lands on the real, fixable cause. Grouping failures by a likely driver, such as source system, is exactly how the lesson's worked example narrows 4,000 null emails down to one intake channel.

questions.code:
UPDATE customers
SET state_code = 'CA'
WHERE state_code IN ('Calif.', 'California', 'CALIF')
  AND state_code <> 'CA';
questions.prompt: This standardization UPDATE is run twice in a row against the same table, with no new data arriving in between. What happens the second time it runs, per Lesson 24?
options: Nothing further changes — the WHERE clause only matches rows that still need the fix, which is exactly what makes the script idempotent
Every row already corrected to 'CA' gets a second 'CA' value appended to it
The second run throws an error, because state_code was already updated once
The second run reverts the column back to its original uncleaned values
questions.explain: The AND state_code <> 'CA' condition means once a row is corrected to 'CA', it no longer matches the WHERE clause on a later run. Lesson 24 calls this idempotent — safe to run more than once without changing the result further, which matters because cleansing scripts get re-run against new loads, backfills, and bug fixes.

questions.prompt: Put Lesson 25's five stages of a remediation workflow in the correct order.
items: Detect — a rule check or monitoring alert finds a violation
Triage — severity and urgency are decided
Assign — the issue goes to whoever owns the data or system producing it
Fix — root cause analysis happens and a cleansing operation runs if needed
Verify — the original rule or check is re-run to confirm the violation is actually gone
questions.explain: A remediation workflow runs detect, triage, assign, fix, then verify. Skipping verify is the most common and most expensive shortcut — an issue marked 'fixed' that was never re-checked creates false confidence, which is worse than an issue that's still openly flagged.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 26, a metric that is technically still passing but is quietly getting worse over time — a NULL rate creeping from 1% to 3% to 6% without ever crossing a hard threshold — is called ________.
questions.explain: Drift is a metric slowly worsening over time without crossing a hard threshold yet. Lesson 26 names it as one of three things worth monitoring beyond simple pass/fail rates, alongside data quality metrics and pipeline health, specifically because a hard threshold alone wouldn't surface it before it becomes a real problem.

questions.prompt: Match each Lesson 27 term to what it actually is.
right: A colored label (on track / at risk / behind) judged against a threshold
Power BI's term for one tracked metric with a current value and target
A status-at-a-glance view built for executives: current value, target, status, trend
A more detailed view built for analysts to investigate, with drill-through to failing rows
questions.explain: A scorecard is the status-at-a-glance view for stakeholders who need status, not mechanics. A dashboard is the more detailed view underneath it, for anyone investigating why a metric is at risk. A status pill is the colored on-track/at-risk/behind label judged against a threshold. A Goal is Power BI's own term for one tracked metric with a current value and target — the same structure a data quality scorecard needs, just built for general business goals.

questions.prompt: An issue's status was moved directly from 'Resolved' to 'Closed', skipping 'Verified' entirely. Per Lesson 28, what's the risk in doing that?
options: A fix that was applied but never actually re-confirmed against the original detection check creates false confidence — it might not have actually worked
There's no real risk — 'Verified' and 'Closed' mean the same thing in the standard lifecycle
The issue record becomes permanently uneditable once it reaches 'Resolved'
Skipping 'Verified' automatically downgrades the issue's severity
questions.explain: Verified means the original detection check has been re-run and confirmed passing — the same 'verify' stage from Lesson 25's remediation workflow, applied to issue tracking. Jumping from Resolved straight to Closed without that re-check is the same shortcut Lesson 25 warns about: a fix that was never actually confirmed is a liability, not a resolution.

questions.prompt: At the fictional Northfield Outfitters in Lesson 29, select every true statement about the customer-data case study.
options: The 1.4 million customer rows versus roughly 600,000 real households pointed to a uniqueness problem
Name casing differing between 'Jane Smith' and 'SMITH, JANE' across the two source systems was a consistency problem
POS-sourced rows frequently missing an email address was a completeness problem
The root cause was random data-entry error by in-store cashiers
A deduplication pass alone, without rewriting the nightly load, would have permanently fixed the duplicate-row problem
questions.explain: The case study touched three dimensions together: uniqueness (one real customer represented as multiple rows), consistency (the same name formatted differently between systems), and completeness (POS rows frequently missing email). The actual root cause was structural, not random error — the two systems were integrated without a shared customer identifier, and the nightly load appended rather than merged records. A cleansing-only fix without rewriting the load to upsert against a cross-system match key would have worked for exactly one day, since the same append logic would keep re-creating duplicates.

questions.prompt: At the fictional Ashgrove Components in Lesson 30, 44 AP transactions existed in the subledger but never reached the GL: 12 were rejected by a retired cost-center code, and 32 were entered after the nightly extract already ran. Which two dimensions do these two causes respectively point to?
options: Validity (the retired cost-center code) and timeliness (the late-entered transactions missed by the extract's run time)
Accuracy (the retired cost-center code) and completeness (the late-entered transactions)
Uniqueness (the retired cost-center code) and consistency (the late-entered transactions)
Completeness for both causes, since both resulted in missing GL rows
questions.explain: Lesson 30 maps each cause to a specific dimension: a cost-center code that doesn't exist in the current valid list is a validity failure (the GL posting job silently rejected those rows), and transactions entered after the extract job already ran is a timeliness failure (the extract's run time, not the transactions themselves, was the problem). Both fed into an overall completeness symptom — missing GL rows — but the two root causes behind that symptom were genuinely different dimensions requiring different fixes.
